note: Candidate adds "which project toward the sea" and "bringing up", which the source lacks.
replacement: In the same summer, after Lesbos had been reduced, the Athenians under Nicias, son of Niceratus, made an expedition against the island of Minoa. It lies off Megara, and the Megarians used it as a fortified post, having built a tower on it. Nicias wanted the Athenians to keep up their blockade from this nearer station instead of from Budorum and Salamis. He meant to stop the Peloponnesian galleys and privateers from slipping out of the island unobserved, as they had been in the habit of doing, and at the same time to keep anything from coming into Megara. So he first took two towers projecting on the side of Nisaea, by engines from the sea, and cleared the entrance to the channel between the island and the shore. He then cut off all communication by building a wall on the mainland, at the point where a bridge over a morass allowed reinforcements to be thrown into the island, which was not far from the continent. A few days were enough to finish this. After that he raised some works on the island itself, left a garrison there, and withdrew with his forces.

note: Dangling "Having thus shown it" makes the Plataeans the subject and blurs "alone did not Medize".
replacement: “Meanwhile we have plainly shown that it was not for the sake of the Hellenes that you alone then did not Medize, but because the Athenians did not Medize either, and you wished to side with them and be against the rest. Yet you now claim the benefit of good deeds done to please your neighbors. This cannot be admitted. You chose the Athenians, and with them you must stand or fall. Nor can you plead the league then made and claim that it should now protect you. You abandoned that league, and offended against it by helping, instead of hindering, the subjugation of the Aeginetans and other members of it. You did so not under compulsion, but while enjoying the same institutions that you enjoy to the present hour, with no one forcing you as in our case. Lastly, before you were blockaded, an invitation was addressed to you to be neutral and join neither party. This you did not accept. Who then more justly merit the detestation of the Hellenes than you, who sought their ruin under the mask of honor? The former virtues that you allege you now show not to be proper to your character. The real bent of your nature has at length been damningly proved: when the Athenians took the path of injustice, you followed them.

note: Candidate reverses who received service: source says the judges asked whether they had received service from the Plataeans.
replacement: Such were the words of the Thebans. The Lacedaemonian judges decided that the question whether they had received any service from the Plataeans in the war was a fair one for them to put. They had always invited the Plataeans to be neutral, in keeping with the original covenant of Pausanias after the defeat of the Mede, and had again offered them the same conditions definitely before the blockade. The Plataeans had refused this offer, and the judges conceived that, by the loyalty of their own intention, they were now released from the covenant. Having, as they considered, suffered evil at the hands of the Plataeans, they brought them in again one by one and asked each of them the same question, that is, whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and allies any service in the war. When a man said that he had not, they took him out and slew him, without exception. The Plataeans thus massacred numbered not less than two hundred, together with twenty-five Athenians who had shared in the siege. The women were taken as slaves. The Thebans gave the city for about a year to some political emigrants from Megara and to the surviving Plataeans of their own party to inhabit. Afterward they razed it to the ground from the very foundations. Next to the precinct of Hera they built an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around above and below, using for this purpose the roofs and doors of the Plataeans. Of the rest of the materials in the wall, the brass and the iron, they made couches, which they dedicated to Hera, and for her they also built a stone chapel a hundred feet square. The land they confiscated and let out on a ten years’ lease to Theban occupiers. The Lacedaemonians’ adverse attitude in the whole Plataean affair was adopted mainly to please the Thebans, who were thought to be useful in the war then raging. Such was the end of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after she became the ally of Athens.
